cards.heading: Protecting privileged mode
cards.body: 'enable secret' stores a strong hash (type 5 MD5, or 8/9 on newer IOS). The older 'enable password' is stored in clear text (or weak type 7). If both exist, the secret is used.
cards.example:
enable secret Sup3r$ecret
!  shows as: enable secret 5 $1$mERr$hx5rVt7rPNoS4wqbXKX7m0

cards.heading: Console and VTY lines
cards.body: A line password plus 'login' asks for that password. 'login local' asks for a username and password from the local user database instead, so each admin has an account. exec-timeout logs idle sessions out. A line needs both a password and 'login' to ask for it; 'no login' turns authentication off completely, so anyone gets in. In 'username admin secret Cisco123!' the secret is stored as a one-way hash, while 'username ... password' stores clear text (or type 7); add 'privilege 15' for full access.
cards.example:
line console 0
 password C0nsole!
 login
 exec-timeout 5 0
username admin secret Adm1n!Pass
line vty 0 4
 login local

cards.heading: service password-encryption
cards.body: Encrypts the clear-text passwords in the configuration (line passwords, enable password) with type 7. It only stops someone reading them over your shoulder: type 7 is easily reversed. It doesn't affect secrets, which are hashed anyway.

cards.heading: Password policy
cards.body: Good policy favours long passphrases over forced complexity, checks new passwords against known-breached lists, avoids reuse, and locks accounts after repeated failures. IOS can enforce a minimum length: 'security passwords min-length 10'. Length adds the most guessing work: a long passphrase such as correct-horse-battery-staple-92 beats a short password with symbol substitutions, which is in every dictionary. Lockout limits online guessing. Reusing a password is risky because stolen password lists are tried against other sites (credential stuffing); unique passwords, a password manager and MFA limit the damage.

cards.heading: Password alternatives
cards.body: Multi-factor authentication combines factors from different categories: something you know (password, PIN), something you have (phone app, token, smart card) and something you are (fingerprint, face). Digital certificates and biometrics can replace passwords altogether. Two passwords are still one factor; a password plus a one-time code from a phone app is two.
